title: Causal Attribution in AI Incidents: Technical Failure vs. Governance Failure Decomposition

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if most incidents have significant governance causation, this shifts cost-effectiveness balance toward governance investment, a high-leverage finding for the field.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: applying a structured root cause analysis protocol to incidents requires careful judgment, manageable with guidance on the coding protocol.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: coding 30-50 incidents with a structured causal attribution protocol requires thorough work but has clear methodology and stopping criteria.

novelty.reasoning: 'Who is Responsible When AI Fails?' (arXiv:2504.01029, 2025) provides a taxonomy with 6 categories of 17 causes and 5 categories of 8 responsible entities, including AI technical causes, developer causes, organizational causes, and governmental causes. Simon Mylius published 'Root Cause Analysis of AI Safety Incidents' applying structured RCA to AI. The finding that '80% of AI failures are process issues, not technical problems' (amitkoth.com) directly addresses the technical vs. governance decomposition. 'A taxonomic system for failure cause analysis of open source AI incidents' (arXiv:2211.07280) provides a cause taxonomy. The core research question — what fraction of incidents are technical vs. governance failures — has been substantially addressed, though applying a specific structured RCA protocol to AIAAIC data at scale retains some methodological novelty.
